I want to be careful about what I am arguing. I am not claiming anyone set out to kill Prisciliano Trejo Ricano. I am saying the arrangement makes deaths like his predictable and makes responsibility for them almost impossible to locate. The second claim is why this keeps happening.

ICE has long had a mechanism that turns a counted death into an uncounted one, it carried a review requirement that appears never to have been used, it removed that requirement in June, and in July it released a 29-year-old from custody while he lay hospitalized with acute leukemia.

DHS called the change common sense: when an individual is no longer in ICE custody, ICE will no longer be responsible for monitoring or reviewing deaths that may occur. The 2021 policy being removed existed to stop the agency from releasing gravely ill people to avoid accountability.

ICE Directive 11003.5 allowed review of a death occurring within 30 days of release from custody, but the review was discretionary, and the ACLU report found no evidence that ICE had ever ordered one in the history of the policy.

Category two is people who nearly died inside and survived, and nobody counts them. A 2022 survey of 85 clinicians covering roughly 1,300 patients released from ICE detention found that every single one had adverse health conditions related to their time in custody.

Category one is people who die in ICE custody. ICE is required to report these, so they are the deaths we argue about. At least 51 people have died in ICE detention since January 2025 by my count, more than the previous administration recorded across four years.

In April I published a framework for reading these deaths, because the official count has never been the whole picture. There are three groups of people harmed by detention and only one of them is systematically counted.

@aclu.org, Physicians for Human Rights, and @weareoversight.bsky.social documented at least three cases between 2019 and 2021 in which ICE released a detained person during hospitalization shortly before they died, and a New York Times investigation found the same practice under Obama.
Because he was released before he died, his death falls outside ICE's count of people who died in ICE custody, and the only thing that changed on July 16 was his custody classification.

Heba Gowayed is totally right, and there is a robust literature for it. Bureaucratic violence is harm administered without overt force, through decision-making, paperwork, inaction, and exclusion. It reads as separate stories because responsibility is distributed in ways that avoid accountability.

Category three is people who die after release, from conditions caused or worsened by detention. Prisciliano Trejo Ricano belongs to category three. So does anyone whose chronic illness went untreated inside and finished its course outside.

After he was moved to a hospital, ICE released him from custody on an order of recognizance on July 16, according to a DHS spokesperson, and he died days later. His family says he was already in a coma by the time the release went through.

Prisciliano Trejo Ricano was 29 and had lived in Durham, North Carolina since arriving from Mexico at age three. He was detained this summer at Stewart Detention Center in Georgia and diagnosed with acute leukemia while inside.
